entries.previousTitle: Zero-Sum Bias – when you think someone’s gain is your loss
entries.title: Zero-Sum Bias – when we see competition where gains can coexist
entries.description:
Zero-sum bias is our tendency to treat a non-zero-sum situation as if every gain for one side must create a matching loss for another. Sometimes resources really are fixed. The bias appears when we import that logic into a situation where several people could succeed, both sides could benefit, or the resource is not actually capped. Our brain has apparently opened a competition before checking whether anyone needed one.

Where can it show up?
- Grading – under an absolute standard, we may assume that many high grades already given mean fewer high grades remain, even when grades are not rationed.
- Trade and negotiation – we may assume that if the seller benefits, the buyer must have lost, or the other way around, even when an exchange can help both sides.
- Knowledge and collaboration – sharing an idea, method, or credit can feel like giving away a fixed slice, although useful knowledge can spread without disappearing from the person who shared it.
- Teams and organizations – we may turn recognition, learning, or improvement into a rivalry even when the real constraint is not zero-sum.

A better check
- Name the scarce resource. What exactly is fixed? Money, seats, time, attention, status, or something else?
- Ask whether one side's gain mechanically reduces what remains for the other side.
- Write down a possible outcome where both sides gain. If that outcome is feasible, the situation is not strictly zero-sum.
- Separate real scarcity from assumed scarcity. Some competitions really do have one trophy. Not every meeting does.

Zero-sum thinking can be correct when the rules truly fix the total payoff. The useful question is not 'Am I being competitive?' It is 'Did I verify that there is a fixed pie before I started fighting over the slices?'
entries.reason: The previous page used broad economic, promotion, and relationship examples as if all were clear instances of the effect. This revision anchors the page in the original non-zero-sum grading paradigm, separates real scarcity from assumed scarcity, and adds evidence-aligned practical checks.
